fallacies.name: Personal Attack
fallacies.definition: Attacking the person instead of addressing their argument.
fallacies.example: "Tomato says my blade matches the cuts in the missing carrot. But look at his bruised skin - why trust someone that rotten?"

fallacies.name: Bandwagon
fallacies.definition: Claiming something is true because many people believe it.
fallacies.example: "Chef, every utensil in the drawer believes Tomato stole the salt. They can't all be wrong!"

fallacies.name: Appeal to Pity
fallacies.definition: Using sympathy in place of relevant evidence.
fallacies.example: "Please don't find me guilty of shredding the recipe, Chef. My handle is cracked, and I've already had such a difficult week!"

fallacies.name: Appeal to Irrelevant Authority
fallacies.definition: Treating someone's opinion as proof when they lack relevant expertise.
fallacies.example: "The refrigerator's ice dispenser says Tomato stole the flour. It's an expert at making ice, so its judgment about theft must be correct."

fallacies.name: False Dilemma
fallacies.definition: Presenting only two choices when other possibilities exist.
fallacies.example: "Chef, either you find Tomato guilty of spilling the oil, or you're saying that spilling oil on the floor is acceptable."

fallacies.name: Hasty Generalization
fallacies.definition: Drawing a broad conclusion from too little evidence.
fallacies.example: "One tomato rolled off the counter yesterday. That proves tomatoes can't control where they go, so this Tomato must have rolled into the cake."

fallacies.name: Straw Man
fallacies.definition: Distorting someone's argument to make it easier to attack.
fallacies.example: Tomato: "The peeler should be kept in a protective cover." Peeler: "Tomato wants every gadget locked away forever so nobody can cook!"

fallacies.name: Red Herring
fallacies.definition: Introducing an irrelevant issue to distract from the original question.
fallacies.example: "Tomato asks why there's frosting caught in my whisk wires. But Chef, shouldn't we be discussing how filthy the oven is?"

fallacies.name: Whataboutism
fallacies.definition: Deflecting criticism by pointing to someone else's similar wrongdoing.
fallacies.example: "Tomato accuses me of dripping grease onto the recipe. But he dripped juice onto the shopping list yesterday!"

fallacies.name: Circular Reasoning
fallacies.definition: Using the conclusion itself as support for the conclusion.
fallacies.example: "My account of the missing cheese is accurate because I'm a reliable grater. You can tell I'm reliable because my account is accurate."

fallacies.name: Appeal to Ignorance
fallacies.definition: Claiming something is true because it has not been proven false, or vice versa.
fallacies.example: "Tomato can't prove he never entered the pantry last night. Therefore, he entered it and stole the sugar."

fallacies.name: False Cause
fallacies.definition: Assuming that because one event followed another, the first caused the second.
fallacies.example: "The soup curdled immediately after Tomato rolled beside the stove. His arrival must have curdled it!"

fallacies.name: Slippery Slope
fallacies.definition: Claiming one step will lead to an extreme outcome without enough support.
fallacies.example: "If you let Tomato keep that stolen basil leaf, next he'll take a whole bunch, then empty the pantry, and soon there won't be a single ingredient left!"

fallacies.name: False Analogy
fallacies.definition: Treating two things as equivalent despite differences that matter.
fallacies.example: "Chef, you throw away empty tomato cans. This Tomato has no filling inside him either, so you should throw him away too!"

fallacies.name: Equivocation
fallacies.definition: Switching between different meanings of the same word during an argument.
fallacies.example: "Chef said we need a sharp witness. My blades are sharp, so my testimony must be the most intelligent."

fallacies.name: Loaded Question
fallacies.definition: Asking a question that assumes an unproven claim.
fallacies.example: "Tomato, where did you hide the measuring spoon you stole?" (It hasn't been established that Tomato stole it.)

fallacies.name: Cherry-Picking
fallacies.definition: Selecting evidence that supports a claim while ignoring relevant evidence against it.
fallacies.example: "This camera image shows Tomato beside the broken plate!" (The gadget skips the next frame, which shows its own cord pulling the plate off the counter.)

fallacies.name: Moving the Goalposts
fallacies.definition: Changing the standard of proof after the original standard has been met.
fallacies.example: "Show us a photo proving you were in the fruit bowl when the spill happened." Tomato provides one. "A photo isn't enough. Now you need a video!"
